1255578.trap: Ataxia and dysarthria suggest posterior circulation stroke, but symptoms developed over 2 weeks coincident with sedative use.

A.fit: Not here: 2-week subacute progression without lateralized focal signs
A.tempting: dysarthria and cerebellar ataxia in a vascular patient

B.fit: Not here: acute 2-week onset with prominent cerebellar ataxia

algorithm.title: Benzodiazepine toxicity and delirium in the elderly

nodes.text: Screen elderly patients presenting with new confusion + dysarthria + cerebellar ataxia
Review medication list: identify sedatives, hypnotics, and benzodiazepines (temazepam)
First-line action: gradually taper and discontinue temazepam to prevent severe withdrawal
**Acute severe sedation with respiratory depression:** supportive care; avoid flumazenil in chronic users
**Persistent cognitive deficits after drug washout:** obtain MRI brain and formal neuropsychological testing
Offer nonpharmacologic sleep hygiene and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia

acetaminophen-toxicity.name: Acetaminophen toxicity
acetaminophen-toxicity.scope: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, 4-hour post-ingestion level, toxic metabolite NAPQI, N-acetylcysteine indications and timing, acute liver failure
acetaminophen-toxicity.core: Potentially toxic acetaminophen ingestion can be asymptomatic initially; time-specific concentration and hepatic injury determine immediate N-acetylcysteine treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Intentional overdose, repeated excessive dosing, unrecognized combination cold/pain products
Malnutrition and chronic heavy alcohol use increase vulnerability, especially with repeated supratherapeutic use
Extended-release products and opioid/anticholinergic co-ingestion may delay absorption

rows.label: Clues
items: First day: nausea/vomiting or no symptoms; next 1–3 days: RUQ pain, rising AST/ALT
★ **Coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy**, acidosis → severe hepatic failure
Early normal transaminases and clinical improvement do not establish safety

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CYP metabolism produces NAPQI; glutathione depletion → centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis
N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and benefits established liver failure beyond toxin clearance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Known acute ingestion → **acetaminophen concentration at ≥4 hours**; earlier result cannot risk-stratify
★ Plot **Rumack–Matthew nomogram**, 4–24 h; treatment line starts 150 µg/mL at 4 h
Unknown timing/repeated supratherapeutic use → no nomogram; obtain concentration, AST/ALT, INR, glucose, creatinine
Delayed absorption and initial detectable subthreshold level → repeat concentration after 4–6 h
Assess co-ingestions/pregnancy; intentional ingestion → psychiatric safety evaluation after stabilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ At/above treatment line → **N-acetylcysteine**, ideally within 8 h; benefit persists when delayed
Likely substantial ingestion and result delayed beyond 8 h → start antidote while awaiting testing
Unknown time: >10 µg/mL or liver injury; repeated excess: ≥20 µg/mL or abnormal aminotransferases → treat
Recent acute overdose, protected airway → activated charcoal, usually within 4 h; toxicology consultation
Continue antidote until clearance and hepatic/coagulation recovery criteria met; acute liver failure → transplant center

rows.label: Complications
items: Fulminant hepatic failure, AKI, cerebral edema, hypoglycemia, death
IV antidote → non-IgE-mediated infusion reaction; pause/treat reaction, then resume when needed

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Count acetaminophen across all products**, avoid duplicate dosing, secure storage
Assess suicide risk and arrange mental-health care after deliberate ingestion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ischemic hepatitis: preceding profound hypotension
Viral hepatitis: exposure/serology without toxic ingestion pattern

adjustment-disorder.name: Adjustment disorder
adjustment-disorder.scope: Identifiable psychosocial stressor within 3 months, marked distress or functional impairment, resolution within 6 months, psychotherapy
adjustment-disorder.core: Disproportionate distress or functional impairment beginning within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, without meeting criteria for another disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Relationship loss, illness, job loss, relocation, school difficulty; limited social support or coping resources
Prior psychiatric illness, ongoing adversity, cumulative stress; assess cultural context and expected responses

rows.label: Clues
items: Anxiety, depressed mood, mixed emotions, or conduct disturbance linked temporally to the event
★ Symptoms resolve within **6 months after stressor/consequences end**; may persist with ongoing stress
Sleep difficulty, worry, withdrawal, reduced performance; impairment exceeds an expected adaptive response

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stress-related maladaptive coping and emotional dysregulation; no required traumatic exposure or unique biomarker

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical chronology** plus functional assessment; clarify symptoms before and after the stressor
★ Screen **suicidality**, substance use, mania, psychosis; investigate medical causes suggested by history
Full major-depressive syndrome takes precedence even when triggered by a clear life event
Reassess persistence, escalating severity, or loss of temporal connection; diagnosis may change over time

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Brief psychotherapy**, problem solving, CBT, coping skills; strengthen support and reduce modifiable stress
Address sleep routines, daily structure, school/work accommodations and practical resources
Medication generally unnecessary; selected short-term symptom relief does not replace psychological care
Suicidal intent, inability to maintain safety, or severe deterioration → urgent psychiatric assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Self-harm, suicide risk, substance misuse, occupational or academic decline
Persistent symptoms may evolve into major depression, anxiety disorder, or another defined condition

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early transition support, coping skills, follow-up until recovery; involve trusted supports with consent

rows.label: Mimics
items: Major depression: ≥2 weeks, ≥5 symptoms including depressed mood/anhedonia
PTSD: qualifying trauma plus characteristic intrusion/avoidance syndrome >1 month
Normal grief: fluctuating loss-focused sadness with preserved self-worth and adaptive function

adjustment-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR teaching.

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; antipsychotics/clonidine/dexmedetomidine adjuncts only, without seizure protection

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common

anticholinergic-toxicity.name: Anticholinergic toxicity
anticholinergic-toxicity.scope: Antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, atropine, anticholinergic toxidrome, physostigmine
anticholinergic-toxicity.core: Delirium with mydriasis, dry flushed skin, hyperthermia, urinary retention, and reduced bowel sounds after muscarinic blockade.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diphenhydramine, other first-generation antihistamines, atropine, scopolamine, tricyclic antidepressants, toxic plants
Older age, polypharmacy, accidental pediatric ingestion, intentional overdose; mixed toxidromes are common

rows.label: Clues
items: Agitation, hallucinations, picking at unseen objects, blurred vision, tachycardia
★ **Hot and dry**, rather than sweaty; severe poisoning causes seizures, coma, dysrhythmias
Palpable bladder, ileus; TCA exposure may add hypotension and conduction abnormalities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central/peripheral muscarinic antagonism; some causative drugs also block sodium channels
Absent sweating impairs heat dissipation; agitation further increases temperature

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical toxidrome + ECG**; check QRS/QTc before considering reversal
Glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, CK; acetaminophen level for uncertain intentional ingestion
TCA markers: QRS >100 ms or terminal R in aVR signals sodium-channel toxicity
Drug screens do not establish severity; ECG and physiology drive treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, IV fluids, external cooling; **benzodiazepines** for agitation/seizures
Bladder catheter for retention; activated charcoal early only with protected airway and toxicology advice
★ Pure severe antimuscarinic delirium → selected **physostigmine**, slow IV with continuous monitoring and expert supervision
Avoid physostigmine with suspected TCA/mixed cardiotoxic ingestion, QRS widening, significant conduction disease, or seizures
Sodium-channel blockade → **IV sodium bicarbonate**; avoid QT-prolonging antipsychotics in high-risk poisoning

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, aspiration, heat injury, ventricular arrhythmia, death
Physostigmine → bradycardia, seizures, asystole in unsuitable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce anticholinergic burden, safe storage, avoid duplicate OTC sleep/cold products; assess intent after stabilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sympathomimetic toxicity: diaphoresis and active bowel sounds
Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: lead-pipe rigidity, dopamine-blocker exposure

anticholinergic-toxicity.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency toxicology teaching.

antidepressants.name: Antidepressants
antidepressants.scope: SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, tricyclic antidepressants (anticholinergic toxicity, urinary retention, arrhythmia), MAO inhibitors, adverse effects (serotonin syndrome)
antidepressants.core: SSRIs usually start depression treatment; choose alternatives by accompanying symptoms, adverse effects, and overdose risk.

rows.label: Use
items: SSRIs/SNRIs: depression, anxiety; duloxetine also neuropathic pain
Bupropion: smoking cessation; mirtazapine: poor appetite with insomnia
TCAs/MAOIs: resistant depression; TCAs also neuropathic pain

rows.label: Mechanism
items: SSRIs: serotonin reuptake blockade; SNRIs/TCAs: serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake blockade
Bupropion: norepinephrine/dopamine reuptake blockade; mirtazapine: α2 antagonism
MAOIs: reduced monoamine degradation

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ SSRIs: **sexual dysfunction**, GI upset, SIADH, bleeding; SNRIs also increase BP
Mirtazapine: sedation/weight gain; bupropion: activating, minimal sexual adverse effects
TCAs: constipation, urinary retention, conduction toxicity; MAOIs: orthostatic hypotension

rows.label: Avoid
items: ★ Bupropion: **seizure disorders or eating disorders**
TCAs: urinary retention, glaucoma, conduction disease; anticholinergic delirium in older adults

rows.label: Interactions
items: MAOI + SSRI/tramadol → serotonin syndrome; tyramine/sympathomimetics → hypertensive crisis
MAOI washout: generally 14 days; after fluoxetine, wait 5 weeks

rows.label: Monitor
items: Mood, suicidality early in young adults; monitor adherence and functioning
Response over 4–6 weeks; taper discontinuation, especially paroxetine and venlafaxine

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Serotonin syndrome**: clonus, fever/agitation → stop drugs, benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine
★ TCA overdose: **wide QRS**, arrhythmia, seizures → IV sodium bicarbonate
Bipolar depression: antidepressant monotherapy may provoke mania

antidepressants.evidence: Not checked online; established pharmacology and prescribing safety.

antipsychotics.name: Antipsychotics
antipsychotics.scope: First-generation vs second-generation, extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, QTc prolongation
antipsychotics.core: Dopamine-modulating drugs treat psychosis and mania; selection depends on motor, metabolic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and hematologic risks.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Psychosis, mania, severe agitation; **clozapine** for resistant schizophrenia or recurrent suicidality
FGA: mainly D2 antagonism; SGA: D2/5-HT2 effects, varying by agent

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Nigrostriatal blockade → movement disorders; tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin elevation
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist; haloperidol high-potency FGA, chlorpromazine low-potency FGA

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Fever, **lead-pipe rigidity**, autonomic instability, high CK → NMS; stop drug, supportive ICU care
Severe NMS: dantrolene/bromocriptine; olanzapine/clozapine: weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia
Risperidone: ↑prolactin; ziprasidone: ↑QT; clozapine: neutropenia, myocarditis, ileus, seizures

rows.label: Avoid
items: Lewy body/Parkinson disease: severe sensitivity; specialist-selected quetiapine/clozapine if essential
Dementia: increased mortality; reserve for dangerous/severely distressing behavior after safer measures

rows.label: Interactions
items: Other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte depletion → torsades; sedatives/alcohol increase CNS depression

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Weight/BMI, BP, glucose/A1c, lipids; movement examinations; **ANC with clozapine**
ECG for cardiac/QT risks; prolactin when symptomatic; ask about bowel function

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia**; valbenazine/deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors
Akathisia can mimic worsening agitation; increasing antipsychotic dose can worsen it
Low-potency FGAs: more orthostasis/anticholinergic effects; high-potency FGAs: more EPS

antipsychotics.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [FDA clozapine monitoring update](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-removes-risk-evaluation-and-mitigation-strategy-rems-program-antipsychotic-drug-clozapine); other effects established teaching.

bipolar-disorder.name: Bipolar disorder
bipolar-disorder.scope: Bipolar I (manic episode, DIG FAST), bipolar II (hypomania and major depression), cyclothymic disorder, acute mania pharmacotherapy (antipsychotics, lithium, valproate), maintenance therapy
bipolar-disorder.core: Distinct episodes of pathologically increased energy with elevated or irritable mood distinguish bipolar illness from ordinary mood variability.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Strong family history; typical onset adolescence/young adulthood
Sleep deprivation, antidepressants, stimulants, substances can precipitate episodes

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **DIG FAST**: distractibility, impulsivity, grandiosity, flight of ideas, activity, decreased sleep need, talkativeness
≥3 associated symptoms; ≥4 if mood only irritable
Mania: psychosis, marked impairment, risky spending/sex, or hospitalization; reduced sleep without fatigue

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial genetic vulnerability with dysregulated mood, reward and circadian systems

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical longitudinal history + collateral**; ask about prior elevated episodes before treating depression
Assess suicidality, pregnancy, substance use; TSH, metabolic panel, toxicology to exclude secondary causes
Hospitalization requirement can establish manic duration criterion even before one week
Major depression ≥2 weeks; hypomania causes no psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization
Cyclothymia: symptoms ≥half the time; no symptom-free interval >2 months or full mood episodes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute mania → **antipsychotic** such as olanzapine/quetiapine; severe cases add lithium or valproate
Unsafe, psychotic, severely agitated, or unable to care for self → hospitalization
Bipolar depression → quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium, or lamotrigine; ECT for urgent severe/refractory episodes
★ **Avoid antidepressant monotherapy**; lamotrigine does not treat acute mania
Maintenance: lithium, quetiapine, valproate or lamotrigine selected by episode pattern; lithium reduces suicide risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, substance misuse, financial/relationship loss; metabolic adverse effects of antipsychotics
Lithium: renal/thyroid toxicity; valproate: teratogenicity; lamotrigine: severe rash

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular sleep, psychoeducation, relapse-sign monitoring, maintenance adherence; avoid stimulants and substance misuse

rows.label: Mimics
items: ADHD: chronic baseline symptoms rather than distinct mood episodes
Borderline personality: brief reactive shifts linked to interpersonal stress
Hyperthyroidism/substance-induced mania: endocrine or exposure relationship

table.title: Diagnostic branches
rows: Hypomania ≥4 days + major depression; never mania

child-growth-and-development.name: Child growth and development
child-growth-and-development.scope: Normal growth velocity, weight doubling and tripling milestones, WHO/CDC growth chart interpretation, developmental surveillance, normal toddler behavioral variants (head banging, temper tantrums)
child-growth-and-development.core: Interpret serial growth and developmental progress against age, family pattern, and corrected gestational age; a trajectory matters more than one percentile.

rows.label: Definition
items: Weight doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 12 months, quadruples near 24 months
Length increases about 25 cm during year 1; prepubertal height velocity about 5–6 cm/year
★ **WHO charts before 2 years; CDC charts from 2 years** in US practice

rows.label: Interpret
items: Nutrition failure: weight falls first; endocrine disease: height slows with preserved/increased weight
★ Downward crossing **2 major percentile channels** → assess intake, disease, measurement error
Correct prematurity through about 2 years; track infant head circumference

rows.label: Use when
items: Developmental surveillance every visit; standardized general screens at 9, 18, and 30 months
★ **Regression/missed milestones → early intervention**, hearing/vision assessment, targeted evaluation
BMI-for-age from 2 years; weight-for-length younger; consider parental heights and pubertal timing

rows.label: Compare
items: Toddler tantrums → routines, calm limits, positive reinforcement; avoid rewarding demands
Head banging at sleep onset often self-soothing; assess injuries and daytime development

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **One percentile cannot diagnose disease**; stable proportional smallness may be familial
Persistent skill loss needs evaluation; never wait for school failure

child-growth-and-development.evidence: Checked screening ages 2026-10-30: [AAP surveillance/screening](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/); growth facts established pediatric teaching.

defense-mechanisms.name: Defense mechanisms
defense-mechanisms.scope: Mature defenses (sublimation, suppression, altruism, humor), neurotic defenses (displacement, rationalization, reaction formation), immature defenses (projection, denial, splitting)
defense-mechanisms.core: Psychological strategies that reduce anxiety from unacceptable feelings or conflict; identify how the original impulse is transformed.

rows.label: Definition
items: Usually unconscious; adaptive value depends on flexibility, context, and consequences
Mature defenses preserve reality testing and constructive functioning

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **Sublimation**: unacceptable drive → valued activity; aggression → competitive sports
Altruism: meet personal emotional needs through helping others
Humor: acknowledge painful reality through tolerable amusement

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ **Displacement**: emotion transferred from threatening target to safer target; boss → family
Rationalization: plausible justification conceals true motive; rejection blamed on disliking the job
Reaction formation: impulse → exaggerated opposite behavior; hostility → excessive kindness

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ **Projection**: own unacceptable feeling attributed to another; unfaithful partner accuses spouse
Denial: refusal to acknowledge external reality despite evidence
★ **Splitting**: people classified entirely good or bad; alternating idealization and devaluation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Suppression**: conscious postponement; repression: unconscious exclusion from awareness
Intentional lying for external benefit → malingering, not denial
One immature defense alone ≠ personality disorder; assess persistent, pervasive pattern

defense-mechanisms.evidence: Established psychiatric definitions; no treatment guideline involved.

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age, family history; vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval with preserved independence; MCI: objective deficit without loss of independent function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; depression may present as somatic complaints

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, stress responses, and neuroplasticity
Antidepressant benefit develops over weeks despite early changes in neurotransmitter availability

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
PHQ-9 quantifies severity; interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger → **continuous observation and psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal psychotherapy; moderate/severe: SSRI such as sertraline + psychotherapy
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid eating disorders; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation, useful with anorexia/insomnia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after starting/changing drugs, family support with consent
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; depressive cognitive impairment often prominent complaints and variable effort
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

disruptive-behavior-disorders.name: Disruptive behavior disorders
disruptive-behavior-disorders.scope: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), conduct disorder (CD, aggression, property destruction, rule violations, ASPD precursor), intermittent explosive disorder, parent management training, family therapy
disruptive-behavior-disorders.core: Differentiate persistent defiance, violations of others’ rights, and brief impulsive aggressive outbursts; family and behavioral interventions anchor treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family conflict, inconsistent or harsh discipline, trauma, parental psychopathology, antisocial peers
ADHD, learning disorders, substance use can worsen behavioral dysregulation

rows.label: Clues
items: Assess aggression toward people/animals, deliberate fire-setting, theft, truancy, and running away
Callous-unemotional traits: limited remorse/empathy and shallow affect; poorer conduct-disorder prognosis
★ **Planned aggression for material gain** argues against intermittent explosive disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Temperamental impulse-control vulnerability interacts with reinforcing family, peer and environmental patterns

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Multi-informant assessment**: caregivers, child, school; developmental context and functioning across settings
ODD: ≥4 symptoms; interaction with ≥1 nonsibling; frequency beyond developmental expectations
CD: ≥3 qualifying behaviors in 12 months, ≥1 in last 6 months
IED: impulsive disproportionate outbursts; age ≥6; twice weekly for 3 months or three destructive episodes/year

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Parent management training**, consistent reinforcement and consequences; family and school collaboration
Adolescent CD: multimodal/multisystemic family interventions; address safety and peer environment
★ Treat comorbid ADHD with stimulants when diagnosed; medication not routine for ODD/CD alone
Severe persistent aggression despite psychosocial care → short-term specialist risperidone with metabolic monitoring
IED: CBT for impulse/anger control; selected cases → fluoxetine

rows.label: Complications
items: Academic failure, family disruption, injury, legal problems, substance use
CD may precede antisocial personality disorder; adult diagnosis requires age ≥18 and CD evidence before 15

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early parenting support, trauma-informed care, learning accommodations, stable supervision and positive school supports

rows.label: Mimics
items: DMDD: persistent between-outburst irritability, onset before age 10
Bipolar disorder: distinct manic episodes with decreased need for sleep
ADHD: impulsive noncompliance without deliberate rights violations

table.title: Core distinction
rows: ≥6 months angry/argumentative/vindictive; no major rights violations
Aggression, destruction, deceit/theft, serious rule violations

eating-disorders.name: Eating disorders
eating-disorders.scope: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, refeeding syndrome, medical complications, hospitalization criteria
eating-disorders.core: Disordered intake or compensatory behaviors require assessment of medical instability, suicidality, and malnutrition at any body size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescence, dieting, weight stigma, perfectionism, trauma; psychiatric comorbidity and family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Restrictive disease: cold intolerance, lanugo, bradycardia, orthostasis, menstrual suppression; amenorrhea not required
Purging: parotid enlargement, enamel erosion, knuckle calluses; hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis
★ **Syncope, arrhythmia, hypothermia or severe electrolyte abnormalities** → urgent stabilization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Starvation suppresses gonadal axis and reduces cardiac mass; vomiting causes chloride/volume depletion
Refeeding insulin surge shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical interview plus weight trajectory, vitals/orthostatics, **ECG, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate**
Binge: loss of control plus unusually large intake; bulimia/BED require episodes ≥weekly for 3 months
Assess suicide risk, substance use, exercise, laxatives; normal BMI does not exclude severe disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Medical admission for instability: e.g., HR <50, BP <90/60, severe electrolyte disturbance or acute food refusal
★ Refeeding → **thiamine**, nutritional rehabilitation, serial phosphate/K/Mg and cardiac monitoring
Adolescent anorexia → family-based treatment; adults → eating-disorder-focused psychotherapy; medication alone insufficient
Bulimia → CBT plus fluoxetine; avoid bupropion because of seizures
BED → CBT; lisdexamfetamine for selected adults, monitor misuse/cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Low bone density, infertility, cardiac failure; purging → arrhythmias, esophageal injury
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, respiratory failure, edema, delirium; high suicide mortality

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early recognition of growth/weight-trajectory changes; reduce weight-based stigma; relapse follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: increased appetite with tremor and heat intolerance
GI malabsorption: involuntary weight loss without weight/shape-driven restriction

eating-disorders.evidence: Guideline framework checked 2026-10-30: [APA eating disorders guideline, 2023](https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/practice/clinical-practice-guidelines/eating-disorders); thresholds: established clinical teaching.

erectile-dysfunction.name: Erectile dysfunction
erectile-dysfunction.scope: Psychogenic vs organic (nocturnal penile tumescence), diabetes mellitus, vascular insufficiency, drug-induced, PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, nitrate contraindication), vacuum devices, penile prosthesis
erectile-dysfunction.core: Persistent difficulty obtaining or maintaining an erection warrants assessment of vascular health, medication effects, endocrine function, and psychological context.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, atherosclerosis, smoking, hypertension, pelvic surgery or radiation, spinal injury
SSRIs, thiazides, some beta-blockers, antipsychotics, alcohol; depression and performance anxiety

rows.label: Clues
items: Low libido and reduced spontaneous erections suggest androgen deficiency
Claudication or diminished peripheral pulses suggest vascular disease; penile curvature suggests Peyronie disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nitric oxide → cGMP → cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation and arterial inflow; venous occlusion maintains rigidity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Sexual/medical history, medication review, genital/vascular examination; assess cardiovascular risk
★ **Morning total testosterone**, glucose/A1c, lipids; repeat low testosterone before diagnosing hypogonadism
Nocturnal tumescence testing or penile Doppler only if uncertainty or selected procedural planning

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Sildenafil or tadalafil** first-line oral options; sexual stimulation required
★ **Never combine PDE-5 inhibitors with nitrates or riociguat** → profound hypotension
Counseling, modify culprit drugs, exercise/weight management; testosterone for confirmed symptomatic hypogonadism
Oral failure → vacuum device or intracavernosal/intraurethral alprostadil; refractory cases → penile prosthesis
Unstable cardiac disease → stabilize before resuming sexual activity; alpha-blockers increase hypotension risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Relationship distress, depression; ED may precede symptomatic cardiovascular disease
Alprostadil: priapism; erection >4 hours → emergency evaluation; prosthesis infection or mechanical failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; optimize glycemia, BP, lipids; reduce excess alcohol

rows.label: Mimics
items: Low libido alone: desire impaired without necessarily impaired erectile mechanics
Premature ejaculation: erection obtained but ejaculation earlier than desired

generalized-anxiety-disorder.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
generalized-anxiety-disorder.scope: GAD diagnostic criteria, pharmacotherapy (SSRIs, SNRIs, buspirone), psychotherapy (CBT), differential diagnosis
generalized-anxiety-disorder.core: Difficult-to-control worry about multiple everyday domains on most days for at least 6 months causes distress or functional impairment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family anxiety history, chronic stress, trauma, female sex, comorbid depression
Caffeine, stimulants, thyroid hormone excess, and substance withdrawal can reproduce symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Adults: **≥3** of restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance
Children require only one associated symptom; reassurance provides limited sustained relief
Worries shift among health, family, work, and finances rather than one circumscribed trigger
Assess suicidality, substance use, depressive symptoms, and manic history before treatment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heightened threat appraisal and impaired fear regulation perpetuate autonomic arousal and anticipatory worry
Avoidance and reassurance-seeking reinforce anxiety, providing targets for cognitive and behavioral interventions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** after excluding substance effects and medical explanations
GAD-7 quantifies severity and response; not a substitute for diagnostic interview
TSH, ECG, or other testing guided by tremor, weight change, palpitations, or examination
Symptoms confined to another disorder, such as obsessions or trauma reminders, favor that diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CBT** targets cognitive distortions, avoidance, and worry; exercise and sleep regularity support recovery
★ Persistent impairment → **SSRI** such as escitalopram/sertraline, or SNRI such as venlafaxine/duloxetine
Buspirone: scheduled nonbenzodiazepine option; delayed onset, low dependence risk, not useful as needed
Allow several weeks at therapeutic dose; continue effective treatment after remission, then taper gradually
Benzodiazepines: brief selected bridging only; avoid chronic use, especially with opioids or fall risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Depression, impaired function, substance misuse; benzodiazepine dependence and withdrawal
SSRIs/SNRIs: GI effects, sexual dysfunction, early activation; SNRIs may increase BP

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce caffeine/stimulants, practice CBT skills, monitor relapse during medication taper
Address chronic stress and comorbid sleep, mood, or substance-use disorders

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: discrete abrupt attacks with anticipatory fear
Adjustment disorder: stressor-linked symptoms beginning within 3 months
Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, suppressed TSH

generalized-anxiety-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established psychiatric diagnostic and treatment teaching.

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice**; specific to decision, fluctuating
Competence: legal determination; diagnosis, age, or disagreement alone does not establish incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, including life-saving treatment; avoid coercion or abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no available surrogate/directive → implied consent for necessary treatment
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or substantially changed risk → renewed consent discussion

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

learning-disorders.name: Learning disorders
learning-disorders.scope: Specific learning disorder with impairment in reading (dyslexia), written expression (dysgraphia), mathematics (dyscalculia), individualized education plan (IEP)
learning-disorders.core: Persistent difficulty acquiring specific academic skills despite targeted instruction, with impairment exceeding that explained by intellectual, sensory, or educational factors.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, prematurity, developmental language disorder
ADHD frequently coexists; bilingualism or socioeconomic disadvantage alone does not establish a disorder

rows.label: Clues
items: Academic difficulty disproportionate to functioning in other domains; frustration, avoidance, low confidence
Onset during school years; deficits may emerge only when demands exceed compensatory strategies
★ Reading difficulty reflects phonologic processing, **not simply reversing letters**
Persistent effort without expected skill acquisition distinguishes disability from occasional poor performance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Neurodevelopmental differences in domain-specific information processing; unrelated to laziness
Skills improve with intervention, but underlying vulnerability often persists into adulthood

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Difficulties **≥6 months despite targeted support** + substantially below-age academic achievement
Individual standardized achievement testing + developmental, educational, and psychosocial history
★ Assess **hearing and vision**; evaluate language, attention, attendance, and quality of instruction
IQ–achievement discrepancy not required; global cognitive/adaptive deficits suggest intellectual disability instead
Evaluate each affected domain; multiple impairment specifiers may apply

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ School evaluation → **IEP** with explicit specialized instruction, measurable goals, periodic progress review
Reading: systematic phonics/phonemic-awareness instruction; writing/math: structured domain-specific teaching
Accommodations: extended time, assistive technology, reduced distraction; 504 plan when access accommodations suffice
Treat comorbid ADHD when present; stimulants do not directly remediate academic skill deficits

rows.label: Complications
items: School avoidance, dropout, anxiety/depression, reduced self-esteem
Unrecognized difficulties may be mislabeled as defiance or poor motivation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early developmental/literacy surveillance and prompt intervention reduce secondary academic and emotional harm
Coordinate family, school, and clinicians; reinforce strengths and protect against bullying

rows.label: Mimics
items: Intellectual disability: broad intellectual and adaptive impairments
ADHD: pervasive inattention across settings; skill deficits may coexist
Inadequate schooling: insufficient instruction or limited language exposure explains performance

table.title: Academic domains
rows: Spelling, grammar, organization of written ideas

learning-disorders.evidence: Not checked against a current guideline online; established DSM-based educational and pediatric teaching.

mood-stabilizers.name: Mood stabilizers
mood-stabilizers.scope: Lithium (therapeutic range, toxicity, hemodialysis, tremor, nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism), valproate (hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity), carbamazepine, lamotrigine (Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
mood-stabilizers.core: Match the drug to bipolar phase; narrow therapeutic windows, organ toxicity, interactions, and pregnancy risks drive selection.

rows.label: Use
items: Lithium: mania, maintenance, reduced suicide risk; valproate/carbamazepine: acute mania
Lamotrigine: bipolar depression prevention; ineffective for acute mania

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Lithium alters intracellular signaling; anticonvulsants reduce excitatory neurotransmission

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Lithium: fine tremor, **nephrogenic DI**, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism
Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, weight gain
★ **Lamotrigine rash → stop immediately**; Stevens-Johnson risk increases with rapid titration

rows.label: Avoid
items: Valproate in pregnancy: neural tube defects, impaired neurodevelopment; carbamazepine also teratogenic
Lithium: severe renal impairment, dehydration; pregnancy counseling includes fetal cardiac risk

rows.label: Interactions
items: Thiazides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, NSAIDs increase lithium; volume depletion worsens toxicity
Carbamazepine: CYP induction, reduced contraceptive efficacy; valproate increases lamotrigine levels

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Lithium **12-hour trough**: maintenance usually 0.6–1.0; acute mania 0.8–1.2 mEq/L
Renal function, TSH, calcium; valproate CBC/LFTs; carbamazepine CBC, sodium, LFTs
Carbamazepine: HLA-B*1502 testing with relevant Asian ancestry; agranulocytosis, SIADH, severe rash

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Lithium toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion → stop lithium, IV saline
**Hemodialysis**: seizures/coma, life-threatening arrhythmia, or renal impairment with lithium >4 mEq/L
Consider dialysis: >5 mEq/L, confusion, or clearance >36 hours to <1; monitor rebound

motivational-interviewing.name: Motivational interviewing
motivational-interviewing.scope: Stages of change (precontemplation, contemplation, action), developing discrepancy, change talk, rolling with resistance
motivational-interviewing.core: Collaborative counseling that strengthens a patient’s own reasons and confidence for change by exploring ambivalence without confrontation.

rows.label: Definition
items: OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, summaries
Patient expertise and autonomy guide goals; clinician supplies information with permission

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **Change talk**: desire, ability, reasons, need, commitment; invite elaboration and reflect it
Sustain talk expresses reasons to continue; discord signals need to change counseling approach

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ **Ask readiness and confidence**, explore barriers; scale questions uncover why scores are not lower
Develop discrepancy between stated values and behavior using patient observations
★ **Roll with resistance**: acknowledge perspective, reflect ambivalence, offer choices rather than argue

rows.label: Compare
items: Ask–provide–ask: elicit knowledge, share concise information, invite interpretation
Maintenance: reinforce gains, anticipate triggers; recurrence → revisit goals without shame

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Avoid the righting reflex**: lectures, scare tactics, unsolicited commands provoke defensiveness
Agreement with clinician is not commitment; obtain a patient-selected next step
Stage of change can vary by behavior and over time

motivational-interviewing.evidence: Established behavioral counseling principles; no guideline-dependent thresholds.

nocturnal-enuresis.name: Nocturnal enuresis
nocturnal-enuresis.scope: Primary vs secondary nocturnal enuresis, behavioral modifications, enuresis alarm, desmopressin, secondary etiology workup
nocturnal-enuresis.core: Repeated nighttime wetting after age 5; distinguish isolated developmental bedwetting from new wetting caused by urinary, sleep, metabolic, or psychosocial disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, delayed bladder maturation, constipation, sleep-disordered breathing
Secondary episodes may follow stress, diabetes, UTI, or new neurologic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary: never dry ≥6 months; secondary: recurrence after ≥6 months dry
Monosymptomatic: no daytime lower urinary symptoms; urgency, weak stream, or daytime leakage changes evaluation
★ Polydipsia, weight loss, continuous dribbling, recurrent UTIs, abnormal gait → **secondary pathology**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nighttime polyuria, reduced functional bladder capacity, and impaired arousal may coexist
Rectal stool burden worsens bladder function; involuntary wetting is not defiance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **History, growth/BP, abdominal/spinal/neurologic examination + urinalysis**; chart voiding, stools, wet nights
Urine glucose for diabetes concern; pyuria/symptoms → urine culture; assess snoring/apnea
Typical primary monosymptomatic disease needs no imaging, urodynamics, or invasive testing
Daytime symptoms, recurrent febrile UTI, continuous leakage, abnormal examination → ultrasound and specialist evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance, regular daytime voiding, bedtime void**, adequate daytime fluids; reduce evening drinks/caffeine
Treat constipation and daytime urinary dysfunction first; reward participation rather than dry nights
★ **Enuresis alarm** for motivated family seeking durable improvement; requires consistent use over weeks
★ **Desmopressin** for rapid short-term control or alarm failure; recurrence common after stopping
Restrict fluids from 1 h before to 8 h after desmopressin; hold during vomiting/diarrhea illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Embarrassment, low self-esteem, avoidance of sleepovers, family conflict
Desmopressin + excess free water → hyponatremia/seizure; imipramine → potentially fatal cardiotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Supportive toileting routines and early constipation treatment; never punish or shame
Periodic treatment breaks assess spontaneous maturation; school/social planning preserves confidence

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic ureter: continuous leakage despite normal voids
Diabetes mellitus: polyuria, thirst, glycosuria
UTI: dysuria, frequency, positive culture

nocturnal-enuresis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric continence and desmopressin safety teaching.

obstructive-sleep-apnea.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
obstructive-sleep-apnea.scope: risk factors, clinical features (excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring), polysomnography, CPAP, cardiovascular complications
obstructive-sleep-apnea.core: Recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep causes intermittent hypoxemia and arousals, often presenting as loud snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, aging, retrognathia and upper-airway crowding
Alcohol/sedatives worsen collapse; children often have adenotonsillar hypertrophy; risk rises after menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed apneas, gasping/choking, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia
Resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation or recurrent drowsy-driving episodes raise suspicion
Children may show hyperactivity, learning problems, enuresis or poor growth rather than sleepiness
Normal awake oxygen saturation does not exclude severe nocturnal disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sleep-related reduction in pharyngeal tone collapses vulnerable airway despite persistent respiratory effort
Intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic surges drive hypertension; fragmentation impairs attention and vigilance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Polysomnography** confirms; screening tools such as STOP-BANG estimate risk, not diagnosis
Uncomplicated high-risk adults → home sleep apnea test acceptable; negative/inconclusive → in-laboratory study
★ AHI **≥5/hour with symptoms/comorbidity**, or ≥15 regardless of symptoms, establishes adult OSA
AHI 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe; pediatric thresholds differ
Cardiorespiratory disease, suspected hypoventilation, chronic opioids or neuromuscular weakness → laboratory polysomnography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CPAP** for symptomatic OSA and most moderate/severe disease; optimize mask fit/adherence
Weight loss, exercise, lateral sleep positioning; avoid bedtime alcohol and sedatives
★ CPAP-intolerant or selected mild/moderate disease → **mandibular advancement device**
Children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy → adenotonsillectomy; selected adults → airway surgery or hypoglossal stimulation
Counsel sleepy patients to avoid driving until controlled; do not rely on stimulants before treating obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Systemic hypertension, arrhythmias, stroke risk, pulmonary hypertension in selected patients
Motor vehicle/work accidents, impaired cognition, mood disturbance and perioperative airway risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight, reassess after major weight change; continue PAP around surgery with monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Central apnea: absent respiratory effort during pauses
Narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleep-onset REM features
OHS: persistent daytime hypercapnia

palliative-and-hospice-care.name: Palliative and hospice care
palliative-and-hospice-care.scope: Hospice eligibility, pain control, goals of care, surrogate requests
palliative-and-hospice-care.core: Palliative care relieves suffering at any illness stage; hospice centers care on comfort when prognosis and patient goals support a terminal-care benefit.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Patient goals and informed consent** guide intervention burdens; symptom relief remains an obligation
Proportionate opioids for pain/dyspnea ethically permissible despite foreseeable unintended risks

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Ask understanding/values → discuss prognosis → recommend a goal-concordant plan
Assess capacity; use advance directive, then authorized surrogate: substituted judgment/best interests
★ Titrate **opioids** to symptoms; add stimulant laxative for constipation, reassess sedation/respiration

rows.label: Don't
items: DNR ≠ no antibiotics, fluids, nutrition or other desired treatment
Capable patient’s informed wishes override surrogate requests
No nonbeneficial interventions; explain reasoning, offer alternatives, seek ethics review for conflict

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Refractory terminal suffering → proportional palliative sedation, specialist review and consent
Emergency, unknown preferences → stabilize while clarifying wishes; honor documented refusals

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Hospice: **≤6-month prognosis** if usual course; longer survival permits recertification
Medicare hospice election concerns terminal-illness treatment; unrelated conditions remain treatable
No DNR requirement for hospice; enrollment can be revoked if goals change

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

panic-disorder.name: Panic disorder
panic-disorder.scope: Panic attack criteria, unexpected recurrent attacks, agoraphobia, acute abortive therapy, maintenance therapy, medical rule-outs
panic-disorder.core: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of fear of recurrence or maladaptive behavioral change establish panic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, family history, trauma, anxiety sensitivity
Caffeine, stimulants, cannabis, decongestants, hyperthyroidism, withdrawal can provoke paniclike symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt intense fear peaks within minutes; palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, paresthesias, derealization
Attack requires ≥4 characteristic symptoms; fear of dying/losing control common
★ **Syncope, exertional onset, hypoxemia, focal findings**, sustained arrhythmia → medical cause until evaluated
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 situations where escape/help seems difficult, persisting ≥6 months

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Threat-circuit overactivation and catastrophic interpretation of benign sensations amplify autonomic symptoms
Hyperventilation lowers CO₂ → lightheadedness, distal tingling; avoidance reinforces anticipatory fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after medical/substance review**; unexpected episodes distinguish disorder from predictable triggers
Vital signs, examination, ECG for cardiopulmonary symptoms; glucose/TSH or toxicology guided by history
Chest pain risk → ACS/PE evaluation rather than automatic psychiatric attribution
Assess depression, suicidality, substance use; agoraphobia may be diagnosed separately

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ During attack → **calm reassurance, slow breathing**, reduce stimulation after excluding danger
Severe acute episode → short-term lorazepam when needed; avoid with sedatives or substance-use risk
★ Maintenance → **CBT with interoceptive exposure and/or SSRI**, such as sertraline
Start SSRI low, titrate slowly; benefit takes weeks; venlafaxine alternative
Continue effective treatment after remission, then gradual taper; benzodiazepines not preferred long-term

rows.label: Complications
items: Agoraphobic avoidance, impaired function, depression, self-medication with alcohol
Benzodiazepine dependence/withdrawal; SSRIs may initially increase anxiety

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reduce caffeine/stimulants**, regular sleep/exercise, practice exposure and relapse-prevention skills
No paper-bag rebreathing: unrecognized hypoxemia or medical illness may worsen

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: persistent tremor, heat intolerance, low TSH
SVT: documented abrupt regular tachycardia, not solely subjective palpitations
Social anxiety: fear tied to scrutiny rather than unexpected attacks

panic-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR and anxiety treatment teaching.

parasomnias.name: Parasomnias
parasomnias.scope: REM sleep behavior disorder (polysomnography, clonazepam), sleep terrors, sleepwalking (somnambulism), nightmare disorder, isolated sleep paralysis, reassurance
parasomnias.core: Unusual behavior or experiences during sleep are classified by timing, recall, and whether REM muscle atonia is lost or persists.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sleep deprivation, stress, fever, alcohol, OSA precipitate NREM arousals
REM behavior disorder: older men, synucleinopathies, SSRIs; sleepwalking/terrors often childhood

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Dream enactment with injury** → ask bed partner about kicking, punching, falling from bed
Isolated sleep paralysis: conscious but briefly unable to move at sleep onset or awakening

rows.label: Pathophys
items: NREM disorders: incomplete arousal from deep sleep; REM behavior disorder: loss of normal skeletal atonia
Sleep paralysis: REM atonia persists into wakefulness

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected REM behavior disorder → **video polysomnography** demonstrating REM without atonia
Typical childhood NREM events: clinical; atypical stereotyped episodes → video EEG/PSG
Assess snoring, sleep schedule, drugs, trauma, daytime sleep attacks

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ REM behavior disorder: **immediate-release melatonin or clonazepam**; melatonin favored with falls/OSA concerns
Sleep terrors/walking: reassurance, adequate sleep, scheduled awakenings for predictable frequent events
Nightmares: imagery rehearsal; trauma-associated nightmares → assess PTSD
Isolated paralysis: reassurance, regular sleep; accompanying cataplexy → evaluate narcolepsy

rows.label: Complications
items: Injury to sleeper/partner; clonazepam can worsen sedation, balance, sleep-disordered breathing
REM behavior disorder may precede Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, or multiple system atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safe bedroom**: remove weapons, pad furniture, secure windows; separate sleeping if violent
Avoid sleep deprivation/alcohol; treat OSA; review triggering antidepressants

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nocturnal seizures: brief stereotyped clusters, possible postictal findings
OSA: gasping arousals tied to obstructive respiratory events

table.title: Timing and recall
rows: Awake, oriented, detailed frightening dream recall

personality-disorders.name: Personality disorders
personality-disorders.scope: Cluster A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), Cluster B (borderline, antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic), Cluster C (avoidant, dependent, OCPD), dialectical behavior therapy
personality-disorders.core: Enduring, inflexible patterns of cognition, affect, relationships, or impulse control cause impairment across settings beginning by adolescence or early adulthood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperament, genetic susceptibility, early adversity and disrupted attachment; avoid attributing diagnosis to trauma alone
Traits must exceed cultural expectations; diagnose cautiously during acute illness or developmental transitions

rows.label: Clues
items: Cluster A: paranoid—distrust; schizoid—detachment; schizotypal—eccentric beliefs, odd perceptions, interpersonal discomfort
Cluster B: antisocial—violations of rights; histrionic—attention seeking; narcissistic—grandiosity/entitlement
Cluster C: avoidant—rejection sensitivity; dependent—submissive clinging; OCPD—perfectionism, rigidity, control
★ Borderline: **splitting, unstable identity, recurrent self-harm**, impulsivity and intense rapidly changing relationships

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maladaptive trait patterns impair emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning; no diagnostic biomarker

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Longitudinal clinical assessment** across contexts; obtain collateral with consent
Exclude mood episodes, psychotic illness, substances, neurodevelopmental disorders and acquired brain disease
★ Antisocial diagnosis requires **age ≥18 plus conduct disorder before 15**
Borderline may cause brief stress-related paranoia/dissociation; sustained psychosis requires broader evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Borderline → **dialectical behavior therapy**; structured psychotherapy and consistent team boundaries
Psychotherapy tailored to trait pattern; use clear expectations and empathic, nonpunitive communication
No medication treats personality disorder globally; target comorbid depression/anxiety or limited severe symptoms
Self-harm threats → assess intent, plan, access and safety; imminent risk → emergency psychiatric care
Avoid staff splitting through shared care plans; avoid reflexive long-term benzodiazepines in impulsive patients

rows.label: Complications
items: Self-injury/suicide, substance misuse, impaired work/relationships; antisocial traits → legal or violence consequences
Stigma and inconsistent treatment worsen engagement; therapeutic ruptures require careful repair

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autism: early developmental social-communication differences and restricted interests
Delusional disorder: fixed delusion rather than generalized suspicious personality style

personality-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

table.title: Common diagnostic confusions
rows: Reactive hours-long shifts vs sustained mood episodes
Odd beliefs vs persistent frank psychosis

phobias.name: Phobias
phobias.scope: Specific phobia (flying, heights, blood-injection-injury), exposure therapy, situational benzodiazepines, social anxiety disorder (generalized vs performance-only), beta-blockers, agoraphobia
phobias.core: Persistent disproportionate fear leads to avoidance or endurance with intense distress, producing impairment despite recognition that danger is limited.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperamental inhibition, family anxiety, frightening experiences or learned fear; often childhood/adolescent onset

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Fear reliably provoked by trigger; duration **≥6 months**, excessive relative to actual/cultural danger
Anticipatory anxiety and avoidance limit school, work, medical care or travel
Blood-injection-injury subtype may produce vasovagal syncope rather than persistent tachycardia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conditioned threat response and avoidance prevent extinction; relief from escape reinforces fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical assessment** of trigger, feared consequence, avoidance and impairment
Agoraphobia: fear in ≥2 categories—transport, open/enclosed spaces, crowds/lines, outside home alone
Exclude substances, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia or pulmonary disease when bodily symptoms atypical

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Graded exposure-based CBT** first-line across phobic disorders
Blood-injection-injury: applied muscle tension during exposure reduces fainting
Generalized social anxiety: CBT or sertraline/escitalopram; venlafaxine alternative
★ Performance-only social anxiety → situational **propranolol**; avoid asthma/bradycardia
Rare unavoidable trigger: benzodiazepine occasionally; routine use risks dependence and impairs exposure learning

rows.label: Complications
items: Social/occupational restriction, depression, substance misuse; avoidance of necessary health care
Beta-blocker hypotension; benzodiazepine sedation, falls, impaired driving

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early treatment, repeated graduated practice and reduced avoidance help maintain gains
Avoid self-medication with alcohol; include relapse-prevention exposure plans

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks; fear of further attacks
OCD: intrusive obsessions and rituals drive avoidance
Avoidant personality: pervasive longstanding inadequacy/rejection sensitivity, often coexists with social anxiety

phobias.evidence: Social anxiety care checked 2026-10-30: [NIMH](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/social-anxiety-disorder-more-than-just-shyness); established exposure-based care.

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

post-traumatic-stress-disorder.name: Post-traumatic stress disorder
post-traumatic-stress-disorder.scope: PTSD diagnostic criteria (>1 month: intrusion, avoidance, negative mood/cognition, hyperarousal), acute stress disorder (<1 month), trauma-focused psychotherapy (CBT, EMDR), SSRIs, prazosin for nightmares
post-traumatic-stress-disorder.core: Persistent trauma-linked reexperiencing and avoidance with altered mood and heightened arousal cause functional impairment beyond the immediate stress response.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence; direct, witnessed, or qualifying indirect exposure
Prior trauma, psychiatric illness, repeated exposure, poor social support

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Intrusion**: nightmares, flashbacks, distress with reminders; avoidance of internal/external cues
Negative beliefs, guilt, detachment or trauma amnesia; hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, sleep disturbance
Dissociative subtype: depersonalization or derealization; severe distress may coexist with suicidality

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Persistent dysregulated threat response and impaired contextual extinction of traumatic fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical: ≥1 intrusion, ≥1 avoidance, ≥2 negative mood/cognition, ≥2 arousal symptoms
**>1 month**, impairment, and not better explained by substances or another illness
Assess ongoing danger, self-harm risk, substance use, depression and traumatic brain injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **trauma-focused psychotherapy**: prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or EMDR
★ If medication preferred/needed → **sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine**
Prazosin for persistent trauma nightmares; monitor orthostatic hypotension, not an overall PTSD treatment
Avoid benzodiazepines; no established benefit and increased dependence risk
Immediate safety planning and psychiatric hospitalization when imminent self-harm or inability to remain safe

rows.label: Complications
items: Depression, substance use disorders, suicide risk, relationship and occupational impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early practical support and safety; symptomatic acute stress → trauma-focused CBT
Avoid compulsory single-session psychological debriefing; maintain supportive follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Adjustment disorder: stress-related distress without required trauma or full PTSD syndrome
Panic disorder: unexpected attacks without obligatory trauma-linked symptoms

table.title: Time course
rows: Full criteria first met ≥6 months later

postpartum-mood-disorders.name: Postpartum mood disorders
postpartum-mood-disorders.scope: Postpartum blues (onset <2 weeks, self-limited, reassurance), postpartum depression (MDD criteria, Edinburgh screening, SSRIs, psychotherapy), postpartum psychosis (delusions, infanticide risk, emergent hospitalization)
postpartum-mood-disorders.core: After birth, distinguish transient tearfulness from sustained depressive illness and from psychosis threatening maternal or infant safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior depression/postpartum depression, anxiety, poor support, trauma, sleep loss, pregnancy complications
★ **Bipolar disorder or previous postpartum psychosis** → especially high psychosis recurrence risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Anhedonia, guilt, impaired bonding/function, appetite/sleep changes beyond infant-care demands
★ **Suicidality, command hallucinations, infant-focused delusions**, confusion, mania → emergency
Unwanted distressing intrusive thoughts with preserved insight differ from fixed psychotic beliefs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormonal withdrawal, circadian disruption, and psychosocial stress interact with mood-disorder vulnerability
Postpartum psychosis frequently represents a bipolar-spectrum episode rather than schizophrenia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale or PHQ-9** screens; positive result requires diagnostic interview
MDD: ≥5 symptoms including depressed mood/anhedonia, ≥2 weeks, clinically significant impairment
★ Screen for **bipolar disorder before antidepressants**; assess suicide/infant-harm intent, access, supervision
Check TSH/CBC for suggestive medical mimics; mania/psychosis → urgent psychiatric assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Ensure safe infant care, assess support, address sleep; do not leave psychotic patient alone with infant
Depression: CBT/interpersonal psychotherapy; moderate/severe → SSRI, often sertraline during breastfeeding
Severe postpartum depression: specialist-directed zuranolone or other treatment; weigh sedation and feeding considerations
Psychosis: inpatient antipsychotic ± lithium; ECT for severe, catatonic, suicidal, or refractory illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, infanticide, impaired attachment/child development, recurrent depressive or bipolar episodes

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protect sleep, mobilize family support; prior severe illness → antenatal psychiatric plan and postpartum prophylaxis
Repeat mood screening through pregnancy/postpartum; establish follow-up before discharge

rows.label: Mimics
items: Postpartum thyroiditis: biochemical thyroid dysfunction with systemic features
Normal adjustment: transient stress without pervasive anhedonia or sustained impairment

table.title: Course and disposition
rows: Persistent symptoms; may occur throughout first year
Outpatient treatment if safe; escalate for severity
Emergency hospitalization; protect mother and infant

postpartum-mood-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG screening](https://www.acog.org/programs/perinatal-mental-health/patient-screening), [2026 zuranolone update](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000006093); other management established teaching.

schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.name: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.scope: Brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, mesolimbic dopamine
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.core: Psychosis with impaired reality testing: distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum disorders by duration, functional decline, and the relationship between mood episodes and psychosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, neurodevelopmental vulnerability; adolescent cannabis exposure increases risk
Typical onset late adolescence/early adulthood; exclude stimulant, hallucinogen, medication, and neurologic causes

rows.label: Clues
items: Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior; negative symptoms: avolition, alogia, flat affect
★ At least **two core symptoms**, including delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, for active-phase diagnosis
Suicidality, dangerous commands or inability to eat → urgent safety assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **↑Mesolimbic dopamine** → positive symptoms; mesocortical dysfunction contributes to negative/cognitive symptoms
D2 blockade reduces psychosis but nigrostriatal/tuberoinfundibular effects cause EPS and hyperprolactinemia

rows.label: Dx
items: Clinical history, collateral information, mental status; assess mood timeline and substance exposure
First episode → CBC/CMP, TSH, toxicology; HIV/syphilis or neuroimaging for relevant risks/atypical neurologic findings
★ **Schizoaffective**: ≥2 weeks psychosis without mood episode; mood episodes occupy most illness duration

rows.label: Tx
items: Safety crisis → hospitalization; acute agitation → de-escalation, then medication if needed
★ **Risperidone or aripiprazole** + coordinated specialty care, family education, CBT, supported employment
Schizoaffective depressive/bipolar subtype → add antidepressant or mood stabilizer according to mood syndrome
★ Failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials or persistent substantial suicide risk → **clozapine**
Adherence difficulty → long-acting injectable; catatonia → lorazepam, then ECT if refractory

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, homelessness, substance use, cardiometabolic disease; antipsychotics → metabolic syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, NMS
Clozapine → neutropenia, myocarditis, severe constipation; monitor ANC and symptoms; all agents need metabolic monitoring

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid cannabis/stimulants; maintenance medication, relapse planning, family support reduce recurrence
Monitor weight, BP, glucose, lipids; address tobacco use and cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mood disorder with psychosis: psychosis occurs exclusively during mood episodes
Delirium: fluctuating attention/awareness and acute medical cause
Delusional disorder: ≥1 month delusions with otherwise relatively preserved function, limited other psychotic symptoms

somatic-symptom-disorders.name: Somatic symptom disorders
somatic-symptom-disorders.scope: Somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder, malingering, regular scheduled visits, validating suffering
somatic-symptom-disorders.core: Distressing symptoms or health fears require a positive psychiatric formulation, validation, and proportionate medical evaluation; intent separates factitious behavior from functional symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, anxiety/depression, chronic illness, major stress; medical and psychiatric disorders can coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Persistent reassurance seeking, repeated testing, high health-related distress, impaired function
Assess suicidality, abuse, substance use, and medication-related symptoms; avoid assumptions based on demographics

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Attention, threat appraisal, and learned responses amplify suffering; symptoms do not require conscious production
External reward differs from internal sick-role motivation; neither can be inferred from one inconsistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Somatic symptom disorder does not require medically unexplained symptoms**; excessive response is decisive
Illness anxiety requires ≥6 months preoccupation; somatic symptom persistence typically >6 months
★ Functional neurologic disorder: **positive incompatible examination signs**, such as Hoover sign, support diagnosis
New objective abnormalities still warrant targeted medical evaluation; avoid diagnosing solely by exhaustive exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **One clinician, scheduled visits**, focused examinations; validate suffering without endorsing unproven disease
CBT, functional rehabilitation, treat comorbid anxiety/depression; explain functional neurologic mechanisms nonjudgmentally
★ Avoid repeated low-value procedures; **new red flags → reassess**, regardless of established psychiatric diagnosis
Factitious: coordinated team, factual records, supportive discussion; protect dependents from induced illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Iatrogenic injury, unnecessary surgery, opioid exposure, disability, fragmented care
